label: *Miranda* Waiver Was Not Knowing, Intelligent, and Voluntary
motion_heading: {client} Did Not Knowingly, Intelligently, and Voluntarily Waive the Miranda Rights

review_conditions.display_note: You aren't sure yet whether your client was in custody. This section was drafted anyway; pin down whether your client was under arrest or restrained like an arrest (handcuffs, locked car, told not free to leave) before filing, or cut this section.

You aren't sure yet whether the statements were a response to questioning. This section was drafted anyway; get the recording or report of what police said just before each statement before filing, or cut this section.
You aren't sure yet whether the waiver holds up. This section was drafted anyway; get the waiver form, the recording, and any evidence of impairment before filing, or cut this section.

Your client never expressly waived; they answered questions after the warnings. Expect the prosecution to argue an implied waiver, which can be valid if your client understood the warnings. This section is strongest alongside facts showing your client didn't understand, or that the waiver wasn't voluntary.

Your client wasn't formally arrested, restrained, or confined, so whether they were in custody will be decided on the totality of the circumstances. Expect the prosecution to argue a reasonable person would have felt free to leave; develop every circumstance of the questioning (where, how long, who was there, what was said).

Police told your client they were free to leave, but your client was arrested, restrained, or confined. Expect the prosecution to rely on that statement; the restraint is what a reasonable person would have experienced.

Some statements came in response to something police said or did, not a question. Expect the prosecution to argue there was no interrogation; the argument is that police should have known their words or actions were reasonably likely to draw an incriminating response.

Some of your client's statements were volunteered. *Miranda* doesn't cover those, only the ones that responded to questioning or other police prompting. Identify which statements this section asks the court to suppress.

excluded_explanations.display_note: Your client's statements were volunteered, not a response to police questioning or prompting, so *Miranda* doesn't apply. If police followed up with questions after a volunteered statement, the answers to those questions may be covered; if so, change your answer.

sentences.text: The prosecution bears a heavy burden to show that the person knowingly and intelligently waived the privilege against self-incrimination and the right to counsel.

A valid waiver must be voluntary — the product of a free and deliberate choice rather than intimidation, coercion, or deception — and made with full awareness of both the nature of the right being abandoned and the consequences of abandoning it.
A person is in custody when there is a formal arrest or a restraint on freedom of movement of the degree associated with a formal arrest.

practice_notes: Document anything bearing on your client's ability to understand: primary language, reading level, intoxication (booking observations, test results), injuries, mental-health history, age.
Expect the prosecution to argue an implied waiver from your client's answering questions after warnings; the argument is strongest where understanding was genuinely impaired.
